This haiku by Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) captures a moment of serene, aimless wandering amidst plum blossoms—a classic symbol of early spring in Japanese poetry. ---

### Literary Criticism

Bashō’s haiku exemplifies the principles of *karumi* (lightness) and *sabi* (rustic solitude) that he championed in his later years. The structure is classically strict (5-7-5 onji), yet the content feels effortless—a hallmark of Bashō’s mature style. Critically, the haiku avoids metaphor or symbolic language; its power lies in juxtaposition. The spatial axis (far/near) and temporal axis (yesterday/today) intersect in the act of walking, creating a coordinate system of pure presence. The word "そぞろ" (sozoro) carries nuances of randomness, spontaneity, and even a slight melancholy—a key component of *sabi*. Unlike many haiku that rely on a single striking image or a seasonal word (*kigo*), here the seasonal element (plum blossoms) is diffuse, scattered across the landscape, while the human action is minimal. This restraint challenges the reader to find depth in simplicity.

Some critics note that the haiku may be read as a reflection on Bashō's own wandering life as a poet-pilgrim. The aimless walking becomes a metaphor for the *haijin*’s (haiku poet’s) way of being: moving through the world, observing without grasping. The plum blossoms, with their faint fragrance and short bloom, also hint at impermanence (*mujō*), though the poem does not dwell on it. Overall, this haiku is a quiet masterpiece of sensory attunement, demonstrating how the smallest details of time and space can hold infinite resonance.
